title: Digestive Tract Anatomy: Stomach, Small & Large Gut Map
description: Follow digestive tract anatomy from the lower esophagus and stomach through the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, colon segments, and rectal wall.
h1: Digestive Tract Anatomy: Stomach, Small Intestine and Large Bowel
blurb: A continuous muscular digesting and absorbing tube from the acid-churning stomach through the villus-lined small intestine to the water-reclaiming colon.
lead: From the muscular churn of the stomach to the absorptive folds of the small intestine and water-reclaiming colon, the gastrointestinal tract is a dynamic muscular tube. In this illustrated guide to digestive tract anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including oesophagus, fundus of stomach, body of stomach, pyloric antrum & pylorus—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: From the muscular churn of the stomach to the absorptive folds of the small intestine and water-reclaiming colon, the gastrointestinal tract is a dynamic muscular tube. Food is stored and acidified in the stomach, where pepsin begins protein digestion and the muscular wall churns it into chyme. The duodenum neutralises acid and receives bile and pancreatic juice; the jejunum and ileum absorb almost all nutrients across a surface amplified by circular folds, villi and microvilli to roughly 250 m². The colon then reclaims water and electrolytes and stores faeces. The gut also carries its own nervous system — the enteric plexuses — with more neurons than the spinal cord. Within the human body, the stomach & intestines (Gaster et intestina) is situated in abdominal cavity, from diaphragm to pelvic floor, receives arterial perfusion via coeliac trunk, superior & inferior mesenteric arteries, and is innervated by vagus (parasympathetic) + thoracolumbar splanchnic (sympathetic).

The oesophagus is a 25 cm muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, passing through the diaphragm at T10. Physiologically, the oesophagus propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower sphincter prevents reflux. The fundus of stomach (Fundus ventriculi) is the dome above the oesophageal opening, usually filled with a gas bubble on erect films. Physiologically, the fundus of stomach stores swallowed air and gives the stomach its reservoir. The body of stomach (Corpus ventriculi) is the main reservoir between fundus and antrum, lined by acid- and pepsin-secreting mucosa with rugae. Physiologically, the body of stomach mixes food with acid and pepsin; intrinsic factor for B12 absorption is made here. The pyloric antrum & pylorus (Antrum pyloricum) is the distal funnel ending in the thick pyloric sphincter. Physiologically, the pyloric antrum & pylorus governs grinds food and meters chyme into the duodenum; G cells here secrete gastrin. Structurally, the rugae (Plicae gastricae) comprises longitudinal folds of gastric mucosa that flatten as the stomach distends. Physiologically, the rugae allow expansion and channel the flow of chyme. The duodenum is a C-shaped 25 cm first part of the small bowel wrapping the pancreatic head; the ampulla opens on its second part. Physiologically, the duodenum governs neutralises acid with bicarbonate and mixes chyme with bile and pancreatic enzymes.

Clinically, regarding the oesophagus, its lower third drains to the portal system via the left gastric vein — hence varices in portal hypertension. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the fundus of stomach, a fundal mass can be missed behind the gastric gas bubble on a plain radiograph. In clinical pathology involving the body of stomach, loss of parietal cells (autoimmune gastritis) causes pernicious anaemia through B12 malabsorption. Medical evaluation of the pyloric antrum & pylorus also notes that chronic antral gastritis from Helicobacter pylori is the main route to peptic ulcer and gastric cancer.

questions.question: What happens to food in the stomach and intestines?
questions.answer: The stomach stores and mixes food with acid and enzymes. The small intestine completes much digestion and absorbs nutrients; the large intestine absorbs water and forms stool.

questions.question: How long is the route through the digestive tract?
questions.answer: Food moves from oesophagus to stomach, small intestine and large intestine before leaving through the rectum and anal canal. Length varies between people and measurement methods.

questions.question: What is the oesophagus?
questions.answer: The oesophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries food from the pharynx to the stomach through the diaphragm at T10.

questions.question: Where is the body of stomach located?
questions.answer: The body is the large central region of the stomach between the fundus and pyloric part; the stomach lies mainly in the upper abdomen, left of midline.

questions.question: What is the function of the rugae?
questions.answer: Gastric rugae allow the stomach to expand and help channel chyme toward the pylorus.
